paragraphs.text: A [Tieguanyin](tieguanyin:definition) made in 1970 and kept for the fifty-six years since. That puts its making about two decades before the light green style took over in Anxi in the 1990s. Its years place it in the third kind the trade sorts Tieguanyin into, [old Tie](tieguanyin:styles) or chenxiang, which is Tieguanyin kept for years.

The leaf grew in [Anxi](anxi:where-it-is), a county of Quanzhou prefecture in southern Fujian, on the southern side of the Daiyun mountains. Tieguanyin fills most of the county's tea land, and its name is protected there as [Anxi Tieguanyin](anxi:on-a-label), so the label states where the leaf grew. It is rolled into tight balls. Tieguanyin is usually given that form by [wrapping the leaf in cloth and rolling it](tieguanyin:making) round after round.

brewing.text: Tieguanyin is usually brewed gongfu style with water at or near the boil, about 95 to 100°C; the light green style is often taken a little cooler, about 85 to 95°C. Use about 4 to 8 grams of leaf in a 100 to 150 ml gaiwan or pot, about a third full. A quick rinse, poured off at once, is common. Steeps start short, about 10 to 30 seconds, and grow a few seconds longer each round, and a good Tieguanyin gives about six to eight. In a larger pot, use about 2.5 to 5 grams for 240 to 350 ml and steep two to three minutes.

notice.text: A smoother, rounder, softer cup with the fire gone, a liquor turned orange-red or reddish-brown, and often a soft fruity sourness.
